1: Start with the full snapshot: do not filter released_year when the question asks for the most streamed tracks in this dataset.
Remove unknown stream totals, sort the remaining totals descending, and use title and artist as tie-breakers.
LIMIT 5 keeps the first five rows after ordering.
2: Split each artist credit string on commas, then trim whitespace from each token.
The lateral subquery expands each track into its credited names and discards empty names.
COUNT(DISTINCT artist) counts parsed names, not credit combinations. This is still an estimate of real identities.
3: GROUP BY released_year creates one group per release year.
COUNT(*) counts stored observations in each year.
SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () totals the grouped counts; multiply by 100.0 to avoid integer division, then round.
4: Expand each track into distinct parsed artist credits. Give every credited artist full credit for the track.
Group by individual artist and compute track count, known stream count, summed streams and average audio features.
Order total streams descending with unknown totals last and keep ten artists. Audio averages include tracks even when their streams are unknown.
5: Inspect information_schema.columns rather than guessing a duration field.
Filter the actual table metadata for column names containing duration.
The empty result shows that this schema cannot answer longest or shortest songs; request duration and reliable track IDs.
6: Calculate the highest Spotify playlist count with MAX.
Keep every row equal to that maximum, preserving ties.
Order the tied rows by title and artist for a stable displayed result.
7: Use only tracks where streams and Spotify chart count are both known.
CORR calculates Pearson linear correlation across those pairs.
Return the paired sample count alongside the rounded coefficient; chart counts are not chart positions.
8: AVG(bpm) averages known BPM values; COUNT(bpm) reports how many values contribute.
Round only the displayed average to two decimal places.
9: The inner query first selects exactly 15 tracks by known streams, using the declared tie-breakers.
The outer query averages danceability only within that selected set.
Putting LIMIT after an aggregate over the whole table would not select the top tracks first.
10: A positive count indicates chart presence.
Use AND so a track must meet both platform conditions, then count qualifying rows.
11: Use CASE to distinguish positive playlist counts, zero counts and unknown counts.
Group by that classification and compute sample size and average valence.
Compare the groups descriptively; playlist presence does not prove a cause of valence.
12: Group all tracks by release month across the dataset’s release years.
Use a FILTER to count confirmed Deezer chart appearances.
Divide by known chart counts for the appearance rate, and retain the average chart count and group size.
13: Require positive counts for both Deezer playlists and Spotify playlists.
COUNT(*) returns the number of track observations meeting both conditions.
14: Use CASE to create the declared Shazam groups: unknown, high (100+), low (1–99), and absent.
Aggregate track counts and mean danceability per group.
The threshold is a convention for this exercise; it is not a universal definition of success.
15: Keep tracks appearing on at least one Shazam chart and with known speechiness.
Integer division creates decade bins; LEAST places a value of 100 into the final 90–100 bin.
Count occupied bins and divide by the total eligible count to get percentages.
16: Compute each group’s count and average danceability; order by mode.
Describe the difference without claiming it is statistically significant.
17: Group by key, keeping NULL as a separate unknown group.
Calculate minimum, maximum, average, and continuous quartiles of acousticness within each group.
Percentiles describe the distribution rather than only its center; compare group sizes too.
18: Group tracks by release year and calculate average energy.
Keep the number of observations visible so sparse years are recognizable.
These are release cohorts in a selected snapshot, not historical measurements of all music.
19: Group by musical key, including unknown keys as a separate group.
Count each group and divide by the whole dataset count for its share.
Sort counts descending to identify the most represented keys.
20: Combine the four chart-presence tests with OR: any confirmed appearance qualifies.
Count qualifying tracks and average their recorded artist_count.
NULL on one platform does not block a confirmed positive count on another.
21: Group by the recorded artist_count instead of splitting artist names.
Compute sample sizes and average danceability for each collaboration size.
Compare the averages and their group sizes; this alone cannot show causation.
22: Filter to tracks released in 2023 before grouping by release month.
Calculate average valence and quartiles to show the distribution within each observed month.
Do not invent zeros for months missing from this sample.
23: Group by both release year and key.
A window partitioned by release year totals the key counts for each year.
Divide each key’s count by its own year total, keeping unknown keys in that denominator.
24: Use AND across all four positive chart-count conditions.
Return the individual platform counts so the cross-platform presence can be inspected.
Sort by known stream totals descending and keep unknown stream totals last.
25: Classify Apple chart presence into positive, zero or unknown.
For each group, report total tracks and known stream totals separately.
Compare minimum, median, mean and maximum streams; skew can make the mean differ greatly from the median.
26: Select pairs with known BPM and danceability.
CORR measures their linear association and COUNT reports its sample size.
Round the output coefficient; do not confuse association with a causal effect.
27: Select known liveness and acousticness pairs.
Compute Pearson correlation and report the number of pairs.
Liveness is an audio feature estimate, not proof that a song was recorded at a concert.
28: Exclude unknown valence or stream values from the paired sample.
Compute Pearson correlation on the raw values.
Streams can be strongly skewed; a single coefficient can hide outliers or nonlinear relationships.
29: Pair Spotify playlist counts with Apple chart counts for each track.
Compute the correlation and paired sample count.
The two metrics measure different kinds of presence; correlation does not imply one causes the other.
30: Group by both key and mode to count every observed combination.
Use the total of grouped counts for whole-dataset percentages.
Sort by descending count and then the requested tie-breakers; keep unknown key groups.
31: Recognize that playlist identities are unavailable: this adaptation groups by playlist-count bands.
CASE assigns each row to the specified band.
Compute mean speechiness and sample size for each band, without claiming these are individual playlist comparisons.
32: MAKE_DATE builds a date from the validated release components.
EXTRACT(ISODOW) derives Monday=1 through Sunday=7, and OR defines confirmed appearance on any chart.
Group by weekday and compare both confirmed counts and their share of all tracks in that weekday group.
33: Use known instrumentalness and energy pairs.
Return the paired count and Pearson linear correlation.
Interpret this feature association without claiming a mechanism or cause.
34: Compute stream quartiles and flag values above Q3 plus 1.5 times the interquartile range.
Separately count missing fields, candidate duplicate extra rows, invalid percentages, nonpositive BPM and artist-credit mismatches.
Combine named checks with UNION ALL. Flags identify observations to investigate; they do not justify deleting data.
35: Group known keys and compute average known streams, total streams and track counts.
Apply DENSE_RANK to unrounded averages: equal averages share a rank with no rank gaps.
Round only the displayed mean and order by rank then key. This is a result table, not CREATE TABLE.
36: Calculate mean streams per known key across the full dataset. Separately select the top 50 tracks by known streams.
Count top-50 tracks by key and LEFT JOIN these counts to all known keys so zero-count keys remain.
Rank the averages and top-50 counts separately; divide counts by all 50 selected tracks, including those with unknown keys.
37: Search the actual schema for a popularity field.
No such field exists, so average popularity >=90 cannot be computed as a Spotify 0–100 score.
With validated scores and individual artist credits, group by artist and filter HAVING AVG(popularity)>=90, then label qualifying rows Top Artist. Do not substitute streams>=90.
